utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I do understand that there's no preliminary matter, although there may be something raised when the witness is escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. I do also understand that the video that is still there to be played is functioning well now. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to comment on something that was raised last week in closed session or private session but I don't think I need to go into that, it relates to GRM 127 and he's number 121 in the Defence witness list. Mr. Lukic believed last week that he had testified as both a Prosecution and a Defence witness in Karadzic. I can confirm that that's not true, that he only testified as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's hereby on the record -- well, it's a mistake which surprises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. Before we continue, Mr. Mijatovic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would like to try again to play the video 65 ter number 1D358, which is queued up, and this will be the first time playing it so I guess the -- the translation will come the second time we play it through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we play it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to play the video a second time and hopefully we'll get translation of the spoken word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have provided the booths with transcripts of the translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's look at it again and we'll now receive translation. [Video-clip played].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "At a check-point at Ilidza, in trucks of the United Nations that had papers that they were transporting humanitarian aid for the Muslims in Hrasnica, the Serbian army uncovered 24.500 bullets. "Today at Ilidza, a convoy was stopped that had been transporting humanitarian aid for Butmir and Hrasnica. During a routine inspection conducted by members of the military police from Ilidza, it was discovered that the containers carrying flour had a double floor and in this enclosed space there were tin boxes. This was enough of a reason to perform an inspection of the convoy. The members of the French Battalion that were escorting the convoy were unable to tell us what was contained in the enclosed space under the containers. The convoy was stopped and representatives of UNPROFOR and UNHCR police were called in and in their presence an on-site investigation was performed. The containers were removed from the trucks and then, with a crane, the top part was separated from the platform to which it had been attached. "Mr. Popadic, from the inspection that was performed, can you tell us what was discovered in the trucks that were transporting humanitarian aid for Hrasnica? "In the trucks that this morning at 9.45 left for Hrasnica we discovered 12.7 ammunition, 5.000 bullets; 2.9 [as interpreted] sniper ammunition, 19.540 bullets. These were found, as you can see, in an enclosed space in a double bottom of the container. This is the second time that in the zone of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade we find, among the humanitarian aid, that which is needed by the Muslim side, weapons and ammunitions. "Were you able to see whose ammunition it is and where it is from? "All the ammunition is manufactured in Konjic and brought by air to the airport in Sarajevo and, after that, by ground transport, this time driven by the French, in the escort of the French forces, that is. This amount of ammunition was discovered. "We asked the respected gentleman from the UN for official information but we were not able to receive the same due to the explanation that they did not have authorisation to give information. Unofficially, in conversation, the representative of the UNHCR claimed their responsibility is just to transport the containers and that which is contained in the containers is not of interest to them. The members of the Foreign Legion apologised with comments that they were only the escorts of the convoy. The UN police said it would investigate the incident and inform us on time of the results. Who loaded the trucks at the airport and where the ammunition was loaded is at present a secret as far as we are concerned. We do not know how many such convoys have passed, but once again UNPROFOR is red-faced and apparently while distributing humanitarian assistance was also distributing ammunition to the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we've all had a chance to look at the video and listen to the commentary. Do the images displayed and the commentary that we heard accord with your knowledge and recollection of this incident, wherein ammunition was found in a UN convoy under French escort?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The comments fully correspond to the situation on the ground and the specific situation. The gentleman who we see the most here is my friend, the late Obrad Popadic, he was Chief of Staff before me while I was chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender into evidence 1D00358 at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can Mr. Ivetic elicit some information about approximately when this happened and I think the witness said that he was present. Do we see him in the video? Can we perhaps inquire about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you provide information as to your recollection of what time of year or month or year this would have happened, this incident that we've seen on the videotape?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, this is what happened: In 1993, spring, it might have been the month of March, I am not in this footage. I'm filmed elsewhere, though, when we stopped another UNHCR convoy and we found Browning ammunition again and 7.62-millimetre ammunition as well and some weapons were found as well. As for this specific footage, you cannot see me. I know quite a few people from this footage. All of these people are from Ilidza, from the time during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the video into evidence at this time, 1D00358.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, I have one additional question for the witness. You say you can't be seen on this video. Were you present during this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was not far away from there. I was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "I was not far away"? How far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, while all of this was happening, I was between 10 or 20 metres away. As a matter of fact, I was giving a statement. I know that journalists asked me whether convoys would be banned from the Serb Ilidza, convoys of the UNHCR and UNPROFOR. I remember that question very well, so I find this to be indicative. I remember what I answered, that the higher command would decide on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question in this respect as well. Were you called from your office or where you were in order to come and to see what happened? Or were you by any chance there at the very moment that they started inspecting this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At any rate, I was informed and I was asked to come, but my superior was there, the late Captain Obrad Popadic. According to rank and according to the post he held, he was my superior at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you travelled from where you were to this place and then observed what we saw at a distance of approximately 10 to 20 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maximum 20 metres, yes. There are other colleagues of mine there. They were all with me and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D358 receives number D472, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D472 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, I think you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That completes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- used most of your time if not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That completes my direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Groome. You'll find Mr. Groome to your right. Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mijatovic, can you tell us what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right this moment, right now, I'm a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned that you lived in Alipasino Polje. Can you tell us what year you moved into your apartment in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 11 years before the war, so the war started in 1992, so that would be, let's say, 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you return to your apartment after the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not return because none of the Serbs returned to Alipasino Polje, where I had lived. I know my neighbours -- I mean, we checked -- well, at any rate I didn't go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I have a lot of questions for you today and they will be all very precise, so if I could ask you just to focus on the exact information that I'm asking and limit your answer to that, then I think we can move more efficiently. Okay? Now, I want to begin my questioning of you today exploring in general terms what types of weaponry the Ilidza Brigade had. So my first question to you is: Is it true that the brigade had three T-55 tanks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the brigade had three APCs, armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the brigade had howitzers; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember how many?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have a 105-millimetre cannon?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so -- actually, it's a 105-millimetre howitzer as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how about 155-millimetre gun, did you have 155-millimetre guns?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 155? Whatever I would just say to you now I wouldn't be sure, really, to tell you the truth because --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't want you to speculate, so if you're unsure then that's --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a chief of artillery and all of that was in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just asking for what you might know. Now, did you have 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how about an 82-millimetre mortar, did you have any of those?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at least four.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then finally with respect to mortars, did you have any 60-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that every battalion had at least two. As far as I can remember now it was, say, eight all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now would you agree that, at least in principle, mortars are designed to be anti-personnel weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when I say that, we mean that they're very effective at neutralising infantry, not so effective at destroying reinforced concrete structures; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly it might be put that way, but there are exceptions. These structures that you talked about, they can be reinforced to a lesser degree or to a higher degree. If it's less, then a mortar could be used or -- I mean destroying enemy nests. For instance, if mortars are firing from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how many different heavy weapons positions were there all together in the Ilidza Brigade? And I'm talking prior to the exclusion zone coming into effect in February of 1994.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, heavy weapons, I think that we can include those three tanks that have a 100-millimetre gun, then that could be three positions, say, each and every tank is a position in itself. As far as I can remember, we talked about these cannons that you asked me about a moment ago and then we enumerated them. As far as I can remember, they were in one spot, so one position respectively for those three tanks, and then the artillery, the cannons, at a fourth one, so it's four positions at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your best recollection today is that there were four heavy weapons positions in the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be clear on this. If I understood this right, you asked me about heavy artillery weapons. Do you include mortars in that? For example, 120-millimetres and 82-millimetres, then they have their positions too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, in your direct evidence on Friday you mentioned heavy weapons positions and I'm just trying to get an idea of your understanding of how many heavy weapons positions they are. So please ignore what I believe they are. Please tell us how many heavy weapons positions were there according to your definition of that term?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's do it this way. I've already said three tanks; then we had at least two howitzers of 105, that's five; then we said a minimum of four 120s, if I'm not mistaken. Let it be -- I mean, it's four and then over there five, then nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then the 82s. Well, there must have been, say, 20 positions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. That's helpful. Now, can you give us some idea of how many troops, how many VRS soldiers would be stationed at each of these heavy weapons positions, if you're able?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 60, 60 would be a minimum and even a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that would be 60 at each of the nine positions or 60 all together?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. All together, all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now in paragraph 22 of your statement, which is now D468 in evidence, you say: "We had mortars deployed in Nedzarici. I saw an 82-millimetre and a 120-millimetre mortar sometime in 1993 but they were in barracks in Stupsko Brdo Street." My question is: Do you still stand by that evidence about those two mortars at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were in this area. As for being in the barracks, well, that's a question. I -- well, let me be specific. It's not clear to me. You cannot fire a mortar from a building, from barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a translation issue. Would you -- do you still stand behind that there were two mortars in close proximity to the barracks in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be formulated like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now change topics to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, I'm a little bit confused about one of your questions. Perhaps you can check that with the witness. On page 11, line 16 and 17, the witness answered: "There must have been, say, 20 positions like that." And then your second question after that was formulated: "At each of the nine positions" --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I misspoke and let me just make sure that we affirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Judge has pointed out that I misspoke the number of heavy weapons positions. So let me summarise my understanding of your evidence and see if you agree, that there were 20 heavy weapons positions and there were approximately 60 soldiers stationed in all at those 20 positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would be an average of three soldiers per heavy weapons position?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to the issue of your evidence regarding false information being provided to UNPROFOR by Bosnian government troops. Now, you were speaking about the loss of electricity due to a transformer that was shelled. Do you recall that portion of your evidence from Friday? And there's no need to repeat it. I just wanted to draw your attention to it. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P5204 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR document recording the situation on the 13th and 14th of December, 1992. Now, this relates to the event that you were discussing or the days that you were discussing. And when that's brought up, I will read you what's at the bottom of the page where we see the phrase "description of damage." It then reads: "Two direct hits were reported on the Kosevo Hospital complex. Shell fire heavily damaged three substations supplying power to the main water pumping station installations in the western suburb of Bacevo" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it on the screen right now. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have English. If we could go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now at the bottom of that page we can see "description of damage." Is this the event that you were referring to, shell fire heavily damaging three substations supplying power to the main water pumping installations in the western suburb of Bacevo? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In B/C/S it's the third paragraph. It's the third paragraph in the -- on the left side of the screen in the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand and I'm trying to find a link between this because the Kosevo Hospital was 6 to 7 kilometres away from us, the Kosevo Hospital compound. So I don't see absolutely any connection between my brigade, which had no weapon that could reach that far away, nor was there any need for us to target the Kosevo Hospital and three transformers. This has to do with the event that I talked about. This is the main transformer that supplies the city --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with electricity so that these three transformers, this is something that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that this does not appear to be a reference to the event that you discussed last Friday; do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at another report from this day and that's 65 ter 15896. And this is a daily situation report from UNPROFOR covering the period from 13 December at 2130 hours to 14 December 2130 hours. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read you an entry from page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So could I ask if we advance to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I can draw your attention to number 3 where it says: "Continuous affairs." And there is a section in there on utilities. In that section we read: "Due to damage at the Blazuj transformer station (inspected by the Sector Engineering today) only 12 per cent of the city's water needs will be available. This situation will prevail for at least three weeks. PTT has no water again." Is this the event that you were referring to last Friday or is this the transformer that you were referring to last Friday?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really -- this is not telling me anything. I don't think it's telling anything to anyone, this section of the text, when this may have happened. I said on Friday, if you remember, that on numerous occasions transformer stations were shelled, but now which one refers to which, there's insufficient information here for me to be able to give a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The one that you were referring to in your evidence Friday, when did that occur? When was the date or the approximate date of that one occurring?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do I remember the incident that I talked about and why so well? Because that was the greatest quantity of oil that leaked from one of the transformer station --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- around 30 tonnes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, Witness, carefully listen to the question and answer that question. And I think Mr. Groome took you back to your testimony of Friday. When talking about the transformer station, you said -- when I asked you: "This transformer station, was it situated in an area controlled by the Bosnian Serb army or by the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation army?" Your answer was: "It was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. It was on our territory, on Serb territory, in the area of Blazuj, that was the precise location ..." So Friday - and that's what Mr. Groome takes you back to - you specified as the exact location as the -- of the transformer station you were talking about to be the area of Blazuj, close to the Bosna River source. And that's what Mr. Groome brings back to your memory. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question is limited now to one item of one fact: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly because, as I told you, Mr. Prosecutor, there was a number of such incidents and this one is peculiar, the one that I talked about, because of the quantity of the oil that leaked from the transformer station, 30 tonnes, that was a rare occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following: Are you aware of more than one hit or damage to the Blazuj transformer? Did this happen to that same transformer once or several times? If you don't know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know that and I'm trying all along to explain that to Mr. Prosecutor that there were several such occasions and it's difficult to tell which incident happened when. No one could do that. Several times, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Several times the Blazuj transformer or other transformers? I'm just asking you now about the Blazuj transformer, whether that was hit and damaged more than one time, not other ones, this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More than once. That particular transformer station in Blazuj was targeted and hit not just once but several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many times approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, at least three times. That's the least that I can claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention back to this report that we have in front of us, 65 ter 15896. Will you agree with me that there is no mention here that the -- at least on this occasion, that the Bosnian government is blaming the Serb army for this event? Do you agree that there's no mention of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please help me. Where can you read that, that the Serb side is accused of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's my point, sir. On Friday you said that the Bosnian government was providing false information to UNPROFOR regarding the destruction of the transformer in Blazuj. And my point here is that there is no mention of that in this document, is there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this document does not have to mean that that wasn't the truth. I told you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in view of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- the question's very simple: Will you agree that there is no mention of the Bosnian government blaming the Bosnian Serb army for this event? The document doesn't do that, does it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this document doesn't have to say that, but it was so. I told you, the members of UNPROFOR who went out to the scene told us what I told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, whether true or not, the only thing Mr. Groome has established at this moment that it at least does not appear in this document. And I took it from your answer that you did not disagree with Mr. Groome in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to the topic of modified air bombs, and you discuss this in your statement starting at paragraph 18. I want to ask you some questions about this munition. Do you agree that a modified air bomb is a very powerful weapon that carries a minimum of 100 kilos of explosives?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And some modified air bombs carry up to 250 kilogrammes of explosives; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you agree that even the smallest modified air bomb, the one with 100 kilos, has the potential destructive -- has massive potential destructive power?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's undisputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the -- you agree that modified air bombs are propelled with rocket motors; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you agree that the distance of the target of the -- aiming the modified air bomb is a function of how much rocket fuel that's in the rocket, so that when the fuel runs out, the bomb then drops?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now, in paragraph 18 of your statement you say: "The trajectory of the bomb was predetermined and could be controlled ..." I want to read you what you said in the Karadzic case, and you said at Karadzic transcript 30750:

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now move to a discussion of the number of military targets in Sarajevo. Do you recall on Friday you gave evidence that there were 1.000 military targets in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, counting the commanding positions and heavy weapons of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so this is a theoretical assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So when you gave evidence that there were a thousand military targets, you are now saying that was a theoretical assumption; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the number of commanding positions and their pieces of heavy weapons, yes, because I think -- and let me tell you, if I were to say one number, number one or number two, and be very precise, that would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we are at the time of the break. I want to show a document to the witness. Perhaps we can do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can do that after the break. However, I would like to briefly revisit a matter about the transformer station. Witness, if I understand your testimony well, you said: Well, whether the document that was just shown to you, the UNPROFOR document, transformer station Blazuj being damaged and it would take at least some time to repair it, might not be the same as you talked about yesterday, where in D471, reference was made to the damage to a transformer station. You remember the issue, that you said it could have been a different incident? You remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I will tell you because there was a number of incidents that the other one required longer time for the repair --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you remember your testimony in this respect. Do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in the one document - and I do not know the -- your language, but perhaps we could ask the interpreters for assistance - it says the "Vrelo Bosne," where it happened. Now, "Vrelo," could you tell us what that word means in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is the closest location to the transformer station if we want to link it to another place because there were a number of transformer stations. And the Vrelo Bosne means the source of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's the source of the Bosna River. Now, the one report, your report, D471, about the transformer station being hit and being damaged dates from the 13th of December, 1992. It talks about this exact position and the report by UNPROFOR where, as we and you together with Mr. Groome established, there's no question of blaming a party for being responsible for that shelling, also talks about a transformer station in Blazuj and it dates the 14th of December, the day after that. Would you agree with me that it would be a great coincidence that two transformer stations situated at the same place would have been hit and that that damage would have been reported on the 13th and on the 14th and nevertheless not being the same transformer station? That would be surprising as a coincidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, what is your specific question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my question is that where you in your answers left open the possibility that the report in D471, that is, your internal report about the transformer station being hit, could be about another hit, other damage than the one reported the day after that same location, same type of facility reported by UNPROFOR. What I'm seeking is whether there's any explanation for such what would be a major coincidence. People would be inclined perhaps to believe that it was about the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, the log-books from transformer stations would provide the most precise answer because they kept records of all incidents that had to do with transformer stations on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This may be very helpful for the parties if they want to further pursue the matter on whether it was one or two hits to this one -- to one transformer station located near the source of the Bosna River in Blazuj. We take a break. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll wait for a second. If you wait for a second so that the usher returns and escorts you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, I said no loud speaking. I think you heard me. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask that we bring 65 ter 30696 to our screens. It is a proofing note dated the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mijatovic, I want to return to the number of military targets in Sarajevo, and you have told us just a few minutes ago that your figure of 1.000 was based on a theoretical assumption. I want to take a look at what you said last Wednesday when we received a note of Mr. Ivetic's conversations with you in preparation for your testimony. The note is dated the 21st of May, less than a week ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to e-court page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately we do not have a translation, but I will read the precise passage that I want to put to you and if you listen carefully it will be translated for you. Looking at paragraph 9. Now, this document includes a note about what you told Mr. Ivetic about the number of military targets in Sarajevo. The note from last Wednesday reads: "Given the number of ABiH brigades that were in Sarajevo and the number of battalions, if we just compute the headquarters of the same, we come to a number of 400 legitimate military targets for a zone the size of about 60 square kilometres." Do you acknowledge that you told Mr. Ivetic last week that there were 400 military targets in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. It misstates the document and misstates what's just been read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Ivetic could tell me how I've misstated what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to see whether I noticed -- the second line reads: "... if we just compute the headquarters of the same ..." Which I take it Mr. Ivetic considers a limitation in the type of military targets the witness refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you acknowledge that last week you told Mr. Ivetic: "... just computing the headquarters of the same, we come to a number of 400 legitimate military targets for a zone the size of about 60 square kilometres." Do you acknowledge that that is what you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with the command posts of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you -- do you acknowledge that you did not tell Mr. Ivetic about these 600 additional military targets which you've told us about last Friday, to get to a total of 1.000?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke of both. That is a fact. I mentioned the command posts of units and the positions of heavy weapons possessed by those same units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it still your evidence that the command posts for units, that there were 400 of them?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I even clarified. It starts from the level of companies up to battalions, and to brigade commands. These are the command posts I had in mind: Company, battalion, brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dragomir Milosevic testified in the Karadzic case. Would you agree with me that he might have some relevant information on the number of command posts of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he should.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask Ms. Stewart's assistance. Can we please go to the Karadzic case transcript 33124 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'll read you what Dragomir Milosevic said: "So let's talk about these military targets you referred to" -- "So let's talk about these military targets you referred to because you talked about them in different ways" --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no text referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's true because it only exists in the English language. That's the reason why Mr. Groome will read it slowly so that you can hear the interpretation. And if you want to hear it again, then we will read it again to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "So let's talk about these military targets you referred to, because you talked about them in different ways in your testimony in chief. "First of all, you talked about command posts ... at transcript page 32553 you said: "'The number of command posts within Bosnian-held Sarajevo was 275.' "So my question to you is: Is it your evidence that that's the case throughout the war?" And Dragomir Milosevic said: "Yes." So having heard Dragomir Milosevic put the number of command posts at 275, do you still maintain that there were 400 command posts in Sarajevo? Or was that a theoretical assumption?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it came to be missing from the transcript. I was clear. I used the information used by the commander of the 1st Battalion of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army who testified here. He said there were some 25 brigades in Sarajevo. You know that each brigade has four battalions on average, so if you multiply that you get to 100. Each battalion has four companies and that brings us to the figure of 400 men. Those are the facts I based my theory to you here --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as for general, I don't know where he got that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if I could take you back to Friday's transcript. First of all, the question was about potential targets, not existing targets. And it was then clear to the witness calculated what the targets were, not saying, for example, whether two command posts might have been in the same location or anything like that, but it was just -- and to avoid any confusion there, I then said to the witness: "I do understand your explanation. Mr. Ivetic, I'm also looking at the clock." I'm always doing that. "Apparently what the witness tells us is that he deduces the number of potential military targets by analysing the number of troops and the way in which they were organised and then draws his conclusions" still about potential targets. Now, perhaps the expression "potential target" is a bit confusing in itself. Is it a target which you may engage and then what a potential target is becomes a target in engaging it? Or is it a theoretical calculation of what number of headquarters you could possibly expect to exist? It seems that -- and there may be some -- I -- of course the Chamber has not seen the evidence of Dragomir Milosevic beyond what you read to us, but if he's talking about existing targets, then he's talking perhaps about something different from what I understood at least the witness to talk about last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the confusion is in line -- the original question given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So let me read you the question that you were asked and which you gave the answer about a thousand. And begins at line 13 on 21478: "One last question for you, sir: Based on your knowledge, how many potential military targets would you have known to have existed on the part of the territory controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo and what do you base that assessment on?" The question was: How many targets would you have known to have existed? How many targets do you personally know to have existed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again he's misstating the question. It's potential military targets. We've been through this time and again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he's now asking how many targets there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But he's misrepresenting the question that I asked in presenting it to the witness, Your Honour. It's causing confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you please look at page 33, starting line 20, compare it with page 21478 and tell me where Mr. Groome, as far as I could follow, was literally reading the transcript, where what he read is different from what the original transcript says.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right where I intervened, Your Honour, at line 25, on this temporary transcript page 33, where he's saying: "The question was: How many targets would you have known ..." And that's misstating the question that we just went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least part of the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can just get to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's get to the point --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's clear that there are two ways of approaching a target. The one is what theoretically may have existed and what was known in fact to have existed. And that is now what Mr. Groome apparently is asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, let's dispense with theory, let's dispense with calculations done in the witness box. How many military targets were you personally aware of during your time in the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could also include information mentioned at briefings and the figure mentioned there was around 300 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- I stop you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did tell you what I based my conclusions on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. What to your personal knowledge is the number of targets that existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, during the war I learned information from my superior commands, specifically from -- also from General Milosevic himself who commanded a corps. And I heard from them that there were some 300 targets, only when it comes to command posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is hearsay, not personal knowledge of the existence, but rather what you learned from your superiors; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is well understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if I can just say something about a small correction which doesn't make much difference. At page 32, line 17, you said: "Each battalion has four companies and that brings us to the figure of 400 men." Did you want to say "men" or did you want to say "400 commands"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 400 command posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I meant. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in December 1992 you became the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs in the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For information, morale, legal, and religious affairs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you held that position until approximately July of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in this capacity you reported directly to the brigade commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is a senior position in the command staff of the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we have been unable to find any document written by you providing legal advice on the use of artillery in Sarajevo. Is it correct that during the five to six months you held that post, you never gave written advice to the command or any battalion commander with respect to the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only did I provide advice to them, but we also received information from superior commands, from the Main Staff, from Mr. Mladic himself. We received, for example, instructions on abiding by the Geneva Conventions and respecting the laws of war. I don't know why you don't have those documents. I think one needs to say -- in being in my shoes, something that is useful for the Serb side. But I wonder why those documents are missing. It is quite indicative, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to something you said when you testified in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is at Galic T 16790. I would ask Ms. Stewart's assistance in bringing that to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You were asked the following question and gave the following answer: "Q. So that we can be clear, are you telling us, Witness, at no time did you provide advice to the brigade commander about criminal law or criminal legal issues; is that right? "A. I do not recall such a situation." And my question to you is: Do you still stand behind what you said in the Galic Chamber, that you did not provide advice about criminal law or criminal legal issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not absolutely correct. He said: "I do not recall such a situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. That is what I wanted to say at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you recall any now?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I might. You put questions asking me to say yes or no, but for example, I have to tell you the following. We were lucky enough, so to say, to have trained officers. I'm trying to go back and remember. I think all of them were educated, trained officers. What does it mean? It means they went through all the schools up to the highest level of war school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not an answer to the question. You are not invited to say just yes or no. The question was whether you can recall having given -- provided advice about criminal law or criminal legal issues. Now, before Mr. Groome asks you then what kind of advice you gave, we first want to know whether at all you did so. Because if you never did, there's no need to ask any further questions. So apart from whether there was any need to give it, that's a totally different question. Whether there was any need is a different question. The question put to you was whether you ever gave advice about criminal law or criminal legal issues. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fairest answer would be to say that I don't remember. I would now have to try and recall it all. I can neither exclude that nor confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's a fair answer. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your time in this role, was there any system in place in which artillery commanders were required to have targeting decisions evaluated by you or other legal advisers to determine if the targeting decision and choice of projectile complied with the international laws of war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify the question for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, perhaps you split it up because it's a rather compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my question is: Was there ever a procedure or was there a procedure in place in which targeting decisions were reviewed at the brigade level to ensure that they complied with the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, there was always that consideration and it was -- made sure that borders are implemented and that the Geneva Conventions were respected. We never targeted randomly. No one from the command or from the artillery branch chose targets randomly. We exclusively responded to firing positions, opening fire on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is legitimate --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- my question is whether there was any procedure in place where the decision taken by subordinate commanders to target a specific location was reviewed by you or anyone else at the brigade level to ensure that it complied with the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely, yes, to put it in the most simple way. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe the last portion of your answer was translated. Could I ask you to repeat the last portion of your answer; it wasn't translated for us. Say your answer again, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always made sure that we abided by the Geneva Conventions and the customs of war throughout the war, wherever I was. So the shortest answer to your question would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the procedure that was in place in which you or others at the brigade level reviewed the targeting decisions of subordinate officers? Describe that process or mechanism to us.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A subordinate unit or an observer sent information to the command in terms of positions opening fire on the area of responsibility of our brigade. Then the commander or person standing in for the commander, although it was a commander for the most part because they were present, made decisions once they analysed the situation. They decided which unit and which firing position would respond to enemy fire. Then the commander used a telephone line or a Motorola to issue an order to the particular crew, to the particular piece, which was the closest and which could respond to that fire in the most efficient way possible. In short, that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now go to 65 ter 30696 and if we can go to e-court page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. Although not being a part of the question, you again and again refer to engaging targets from which fire was opened at your positions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there may be not that much dispute that at least a firing position qualifies as a target, irrespective of what weapon you would use to engage that target. But what about targets at moments that you are not just simply returning fire to the origin of fire you had been subject to? What about other targets? Or is it your position that, during the whole of the war, the only thing that happened is that you fired back at positions from where you were fired at and you never engaged ever any other target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, never during the war were civilians targets engaged or religious facilities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm not asking that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- exclusively military targets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. Carefully listen to my question. Military targets not being the origin of fire that engaged your positions, so not a mortar, mobile mortar, or a tank, or whatever, or a sniper, but other targets, I'm not saying that they were not military targets, but I'm asking you what the procedure was to decide to engage such other target and by what means and how that decision was taken and perhaps then reviewed by the higher -- by a higher level in the chain of command. That was my question. You are always responding to questions that are not put to you, at least often you make that the focus of your answer. So other targets. Could you tell us whether -- how that procedure was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I haven't heard of a single case of it being asked to target any other targets except for military targets that had already fired at us, if I can put it that way. I do not know of a single different case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are telling us that there were 300 command posts. Now, usually firing doesn't take place from the command post itself, I wouldn't exclude that but that's not the common thing you would expect. They are -- were all potential targets for you. Who did determine -- were they never fired at, command posts? Were any troop movements ever being fired at? Was there ever any fire at -- well, whatever other military target there may have been? Or did that never happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know - I cannot claim that this kind of thing never happened - but as far as I know, we only responded to fire with fire, that is to say, those targets that had already targeted us with their fire. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's what I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's your -- if that's your testimony, therefore, Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, now I'm going to draw your attention to again this proofing note, Mr. Ivetic's notes about your conversations with him last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's 65 ter 30696, and if we could go to e-court page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me read you what paragraph 6 of this proofing note states: "The Witness recalled that during his time in the Brigade, he caused 200 Serb soldiers to be detained and arrested for infractions of army discipline and crimes of larceny. The witness was a strong believer in enforcing military discipline ..." Now, my question to you is whether you personally initiated investigations and punishments of 200 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of this I did personally. As a result of that, that is to say, these constant efforts to exercise discipline and to have full responsibility, thank God the Serb Ilidza did not have a single war crime, not a single rape case. I'm proud of that, and I thank my Serb brothers who showed in this way as well their character and their honesty in waging war. But this had to be disciplined locally. I mean, soldiers had to be disciplined locally. You know what a war is and you know what a war situation is. If you're not in a position to discipline people, they're going to do all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you now please answer the question that was put to you. The first part of your answer was about war crimes. You were not asked about war crimes. The second part of your answer was that if you are not in a position to discipline people, that they're going to do all sorts of things. The question, however, was whether you personally initiated investigations and punishments of 200 soldiers, a question which is clearly linked to the detention and arrest for infractions of army discipline and crimes of larceny. Did you investigate and follow-up for those 200?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of this I and my commander, I mean this number two man who replaced me as chief of security and so on, so it has to do with the brigade so that was in the brigade. Now, how do I put this? I personally dealt with quite a few of these, actually carried this through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's your best recollection of the number that you personally dealt with?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, close to this number, let's say over 100 for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you're aware that there were allegations pertaining to the conduct of soldiers on all sides of the conflict, allegations that all soldiers on all sides had committed infractions of international law? You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you're aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I have to intervene for a second. You are moving away from the internal discipline and that to international violations of international law. You should be clear in announcing that you move to another aspect of criminal law, that is, violations of international law. Because where earlier the witness started saying that thank God no one ever committed a war crime, I said that was not the question. So at that moment you were dealing with a different type of misbehaviour compared to what you introduced now, and that should be clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness, if it's not clear that I'm talking about violations of international law, I'm now asking you about that. Okay? And you've just confirmed that there were allegations of violations of international law made against all parties to the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I saw and heard -- well, yes, that's true. Saw it on television, heard about it, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you aware of any investigation into an allegation of a violation of international laws of war within your brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within my brigade, as far as I know, no, there weren't any such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- you say: "... there weren't any such things." Do you mean to say there was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that there were no violations or that there were no investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, by virtue of the fact that there were no violations of international public law, there was no need to start investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I could just briefly tell you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm talking about what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I am -- you are giving a kind of logic in your answer by saying if such violations have not been committed, of course there's nothing to investigate. However, in real life, perhaps things have a different causal relationship, that is, you can only establish that a violation has been committed or has not been committed after you have investigated any allegations of such crimes or such violations being committed. I just put it to you that my logic may be slightly from yours and your answer was to some extent depending on logic rather than on factual observations. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you to focus on investigation, not on the results of an investigation. But are there any -- were there any investigations that you were aware of within your brigade, allegations that soldiers may have unlawfully targeted civilians, either by sniping or by shelling?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot rule that out after all this time, but I know that there weren't any violations of international public law. Therefore, logic indicates that there was no need to carry out this kind of investigation, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we have the same problem with: "I cannot rule that out after all ..." It's again about -- is it about allegations? Is it about established violations? Or is it about investigations ? And you say there weren't any violations of international public law. Sniping at a civilian target, would you consider that to be a violation of international public law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there was firing at civilians, it is only natural that that is violation of international public law because civilians are protected in each and every case and in every way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to verify that we have a common understanding of such matters. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall any occasion in which General Galic ordered an investigation into an allegation that there had been a violation of the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I can't remember right now. It's quite possible, I don't rule it out, but I just don't remember, especially not of a specific case. Whatever I would say would not be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss some of the maps which are associated to your statement and where you indicated the location of some military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we see D469 on our screens. It is a map of Alipasino Polje. And if we could zoom in to where we see the 6, it's just to the right of the centre of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to read you a passage from paragraph 8 of your statement in the Karadzic case where you explain the markings on this map and confirm that I understand your evidence. Paragraph 8 says: "I have marked with a red circle the building where I lived." First let me ask you, that red circle right next to the green dot adjacent to the number 6, is that the building where you lived?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So back to your Karadzic statement: "I have marked with a red circle the building where I lived and with a red square the police building across the street from Cetinska, Geteova Street." So the red square that we see approximately across from where you lived, that indicates where the police building was; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now it looks from this map that the police building may be the only building across the road from where you lived; is that correct? Were there other buildings or was it the only building?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. You see, there were buildings here where Srakino Selo started. Then there is that school, the 1st of May it's called. I've already spoke about my sister-in-law and the school was turned into a prison and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, let's -- so we keep this in a -- proceed in an organised way. Is your answer that: No, there were other buildings across the street from where you lived?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation that I received said that I should say that that is not correct, but I am claiming that there were buildings opposite my building. Two or -- or three or four floors. So the police station was there too and there were buildings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I'm claiming that it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Are those other buildings you're referring to across the street from where you lived, are they indicated on this map?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in particular marked with red, but you can see this on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the police building that you've marked with the red square on this map, was that police station there before the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've already told us that you lived at this location for 11 years. Was that police station there the entire time that you lived at that location?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that that police station was there during the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you happen to know whether that police station is still there at the same location?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is one but I don't dare say anything for sure. I think that it is more likely that it does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we see D470.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This was another map that was tendered with your statement. Okay. Now we can see -- this was the map that was produced for the Karadzic case. You do recognise it; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you marked this map with circles to indicate locations where you believe enemy fire had originated; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let me read paragraph 9 of your Karadzic statement in reference to this map. "I have drawn military targets at Alipasino Polje and marked them with numbers as follows: Number 1, police building ..." The circle with the number 1 next to it is where you say the police station was; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it is in the same location on the previous map we've just looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why did you consider the police station to be a military target?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, quite simply, the right word would be potential military targets. These are places from which fire was opened. That would be right, that would be correct and concrete in relation to this. These are places -- well, I've already told you about this. The school called the 1st of May is close to this police station. I already told you that at the very outset of the war -- if I'm not mistaken, I said that every time because that's a fact. At the beginning of the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there was a sniper or a machine-gun nest -- please allow me - and then 120-millimetres. So that's nearby, it's perhaps less than 50 metres from the police station. And the school is not marked, and I told you yesterday about this case, that they set up a prison there and put the unit there --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the school the 1st of May and that is right next to the police station -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're talking about the police station now. Is it your evidence that there was outgoing fire from some type of weapon from the police station; is that your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the police station. Next to the police station there was a machine-gun nest and the calibre was 120-millimetres, because you cannot fire a mortar from a building even if you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's for that reason that you circled the police station as a potential military target; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we look at 65 ter 30696, e-court page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this deals with what I believe you're talking about now. In the statement you signed on the 10th of May, you referred to a sniper's nest in paragraph 7. Can you describe for us precisely where the sniper's nest was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this school, the 1st of May, the machine-gun nest and the sniper nest within the school. And then between the school and the police station there was a mortar nest of 120-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, last Wednesday evening we received a proofing note that said: "The witness does not know why the Serbian version states that there was a machine-gun nest nor why the English version says there was a snipers nest. In fact, the witness recalls that there was a mortar nest at that location." Now, last Friday with respect to this issue you said the following at T 21438: "Q. What can you tell us in relation to this? Which accords with your recollection of what was present approximately 150 metres from this school on Cetinska Street?" "A. As a matter of fact, there were both, both a snipers nest and a machine-gun nest at the beginning of the war. There was also a mortar position nearby and that's the truth of the matter." Now, my question to you is: Do you acknowledge that you have changed your evidence with respect to the type of weapon that was located at this location we're now discussing?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that I changed anything. My statement is identical to what I said just now and what you read out is correct, it's identical, so I didn't change anything. Nothing was changed, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now take a look at P6507.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to return to the precise location of where this police station was. That's P6507. Now, earlier in the -- or sorry, early last week I asked another Defence witness familiar with this area to mark the location of where the police station was. Now, he didn't live across the street from it like you did, but he marked it anyway. Can I direct your attention to the right side of the map. Can you see the hand-drawn red circle with the letters PS to the right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you can see where this other witness marked the location of the police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please speak into the microphone because the interpreters couldn't hear you and could you re-start your answer. The question was: "So you can see where this other witness marked the location of the police station; correct?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Carefully listen to the next question. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that we see 30 -- 65 ter 30695 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, sir, while that's being brought up, I'll tell you that it is an aerial image of Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but over here there are some changes and I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, do you agree that this is an aerial picture of Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but see here Geteova Street, I know that then it was Cetinska. Then there was no street of Safeta Hadzica. Then this Sulejman Efendi Music, there are changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We all are familiar with the fact that street names have changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to the next page and this is a close-up or a closer image of the Alipasino Polje buildings that we are now talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, will you agree with me that the circle marked location 1 is the building that you lived in; correct?
