utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to analyse this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Take your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no numbers here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we need to have a -- do you see an oval with next to it in red number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Red you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether that oval next to where number 1 in red is indicated is the place, is the apartment block where you used to live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it should be either here or I mean -- well, I'm a bit -- well, you know, the cardinal points and whatever. So it's either on the left or on the right. But there were four entrances and almost -- in a straight line, one next to the other. Now I see something different here, as if it were a different building, and it should be the building where I lived. Also, there are lots of details --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for example, I see here that -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The circle with number 1, is it or is it not the building that you lived in for 11 years?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, but really it's difficult for me to find my bearings on these maps. It's either here or here because I even --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back then to D470. This is where you marked with, I imagine, some degree of certainty the building where you lived in.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, you see, it's not disputed. It's either here to the left or to the right in Geteova Street as it's called today, that's where my building was. But here, judging from the design of these maps I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise, I called up the wrong map, D469.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, that's now on the screen. Now, you see the building you circled and indicated it was the building you lived in. You see that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps it will assist the witness, I have a clean hard copy of this D469. If he could have that when I show the aerial image. Could I ask for the usher's assistance. And again now if we could return to 65 ter 30695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would assist everybody if you invite the witness to mark the map where he thinks he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'll do that, Your Honour. If we go to page 2 of 30695.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So Judge Fluegge has suggested that perhaps if you don't think that the circle with the number 1 is where you lived, if you would draw a circle around the building where you lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I think that this is the building, that it should be. If there were numbers -- as it is, it's quite difficult for me to find my bearings. It could be this one here or this one -- sir, if you can see what I'm pointing at, Mr. Prosecutor, I think it's the one that I marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We cannot. If you look at the screen in front of you, you can see the aerial image again. Look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it turns out that it's the one and same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so the circle with number 2, that's the location that you marked as the location of the police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't see the parking-lot here. And across the street from my building and the police station was a parking-lot, just a parking-lot. There were no other buildings and I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, sir, let's --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that it's possible that something has been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's proceed just very -- step by step. The circle at the far right with the number 3, on the screen, sir, please don't look at the map on the desk at the moment. You see the circle and the number 3 underneath that circle?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be the police station, this one, number 3, that could be. It has the parking-lot. I think that's the parking-lot that was between us. When I say "us," I mean between the buildings, the residential ones, and the location where the police station was. That could be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do you wish to change your evidence that you gave before the Karadzic Chamber and again in this Chamber that location 2 was the location of the police station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not, and that this could even be the Andrija Raso School according to me, but once again all of this -- many things are new, it could be the school that my children attended, Andrija Raso, but so many things have changed. It's not clear to me. When I look at it now, to the left from the entrance to my building was the school and here it turns out that it was to the right. So this map confuses me somewhat --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I began this by asking you a very simple question. The building across the street from where you lived, your evidence has been that that's a police station. Is it no longer your evidence that the building across the street from where you lived is a police station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I stand by this because it can't be any different. It's just that the buildings and the map can confuse me, that's all. But I assert - I lived there for 11 years - across the street from the entrance to my building was the police station, exactly across the street from it. There was just a parking-lot between us --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and now how it looks on a map or if I can make a mistake because of it, that's another matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock and I have another reason why I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- like to take a break now. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, would you please keep in mind if you say "you're changing your evidence about the police station being across the street," well, if the police station is somewhere else, the next question to know whether it's across the street where the witness lived, we also have the verify whether the marking of where he lived is correct. Still there's an option if he says there was -- "between my house and the police station there was a parking-lot," it doesn't seem very much to be between 1 and 2. However, it would be between 3 and any building opposite that street which might mean that he marked them perhaps wrong in combination, which would mean that they would have lived not at what he indicated as number 1, but he indicated that there are similar buildings -- I mean, there is quite a lot of similarity apparently in the construction and the structures there, that it might have been, if we look at this last picture, in the right top corner somewhere out of the four quarters rather than the left top corner. That's at least something that needs to be further explored before we can suggest to the witness that he changed his testimony that the police station was opposite his building. He may have changed his testimony as that whether what we find under number 2 is the police station, but unless we know whether if that's a wrong marking the other marking may be wrong as well, it's not yet said that the police station was not opposite from where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it certainly would assist in this line of questioning if the Chamber could familiarise itself with D469. I will bring hard copies of both this exhibit and the aerial photos to have for the Chamber. It may assist you in following the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing we want to do is be perfectly clear that we have an exact understanding of the local situation and also make sure that the witness has an exact understanding of what he's marking and whether there's any risk that he makes mistakes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask that D469 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, while that's being brought to our screens, would it be fair to say that as a senior member of the Ilidza Brigade you worked with maps on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's not in dispute. It's just obvious here. I can see it. I had some rest so I see that my building is this one -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's proceed very slowly, otherwise there's a chance for great confusion, and when you point to the screen we cannot see what you're pointing at. So I'm going to ask you very precise questions. Let's just go step by step. So I have D469 on the screen. Your Karadzic evidence is that the red circle indicates where you lived. Do you still believe that is where you lived?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask the usher to assist you and I'm going to and you to draw -- perhaps if we could use a different colour, perhaps blue. Could I ask that you draw a circle around the building in Alipasino Polje where you lived for 11 years.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so the record indicates the mark is in green. Could I ask you to put a number 1 next to it. Can you put a number 1 next to the circle you've just drawn to indicate where you now believe your house is. Could I ask you to do it a little bit away from the circle so we can clearly see the 1.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following: We remove this marking and then a blue pen will be used to mark the building where you lived for 11 years and then we don't need, at least for this moment, a number 1, Mr. Groome, but perhaps later we need that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's number 1 and that's in blue the building where you used to live. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now can I now ask you to draw a circle around the building where you said there was a police station. If you draw a circle around that building and put a number 2 next to it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher stay with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It looks like he's trying to write something but it doesn't seem to be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And the witness already made a dot very close to the structure --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Across the street from my building, that's where the police station was. Now, these buildings here ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you draw --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose it could be here or perhaps here, across the street from my building, exactly across the street from it, that's where the police station was and the parking-lot was between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put a 2 to the right of that circle that you've just made?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we also ask the witness to look at the marking number 3 on the aerial photo to see whether that refreshes his --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just want to tender this and then maybe just ask a couple questions before this new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we tender this new version of D469 with additional marks made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the map now marked with additional blue markings by the witness receives number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P6528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6528 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, sir, so we are clear, the red circle and the red square that we see on this exhibit should be ignored. They are not the location of where you lived and they are not the location of the police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's strange to me that this could happen that the map appeared like this. These are the facts, that I lived here for 11 years. I would leave for work in the morning and I would come back in the afternoon, so I passed there twice a day at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, do you believe that you made a mistake when you marked or indicated where you lived or do you believe someone else made a mistake when they produced this diagram for the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't -- it wouldn't be fair to say if it were me or somebody else because neither would be true, but what I showed you now that's what the fact is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now look at D470.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw your attention to the circle with the 1 next to it, am I correct that now you believe this marking is in error, this does not indicate the location of the police station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, just to be sure, can we now return to 65 ter 30695. And if we can go to e-court page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher, I'm going to ask you to circle the location of where you lived with a single circle, please only make one circle, with a number 1 and the location of the police station with a circle and a number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it should be in blue again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I see that it is in blue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would tender that screen image of the witness's markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document as marked by the witness receives number P6529, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I now ask that we go to e-court page 5 of 65 ter 30695.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this next photograph was taken of the building you have just indicated as the police station. I want to confirm that it is the building you remember as the police station. Is that the building you've referred to as the police station?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 30695.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30695 receives number 65 -- P6530, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Groome, just for my understanding, could I take it that this picture is then taken in north-easterly direction, and therefore exposes the south -- I'm looking at page 2 of the same series.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe you can see the drive that we're then looking in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- on e-court page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mijatovic, do you remember when you testified in the Galic case you were also asked to mark a map of military targets in this part of Sarajevo. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I probably remember or I mostly do it. It was also quite a long time ago, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me show you 1D1814 from the Galic case and see if it helps remind you of that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 30685 in this case. Can I ask that that be brought to the screen, and I could ask Ms. Stewart to give the usher some large hard copies of this. I believe it will assist us all in looking at this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you are now moving away from 65 ter 30695. Pages of it have been marked, have been tendered, have been admitted. Can we forget about the rest or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were always saying this is page 2, that's page 5. Or is the totality already tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I intended to tender the totality of the exhibit when I -- that last statement I made when I tendered 30695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that's -- yes, because there was no further marking on it and you included, then, all pages of that Rule 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you've had a chance to look at 65 ter 30685, my first question is: Is this a copy of the map that you marked military targets on for your evidence in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, do you recognise this map? Is this the map?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say because all the maps are very similar. I couldn't say how long it's been, ten years I suppose, so I'm supposed say -- all maps are quite similar. It was a problem for me to find my bearings a little while ago after so many years because the streets are different, the buildings are the same but -- so why did I get into this position recently, because I wonder why you didn't save a map with those street names that we used then, the street names and the buildings as they were because --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were called as a witness by the Defence in this case and Mr. Groome tries to do his utmost best to clarify any confusion that may exist on the basis of maps, et cetera. Let's take our time and let's not -- let's not be bothered by that it could have been done in a different way. We try to do our utmost best to allow you to testify to the best of your abilities. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the handwriting on the map, this is your handwriting, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You're not sure whether you recognise your own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it is my handwriting, though there are some numbers and markings, but yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can draw your attention, can you find Alipasino Polje on this map?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And will you agree with me that the map does not indicate that you circled any military target on the physical compound of Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could focus or zoom in on the lower right quadrant of the one we're looking at on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it here. For example, under number 1, we've seen maps where it was marked next to PTT Engineering from where they fired from howitzers at us and they would go into a shelter. Then we would fire at them and then UNPROFOR would protest. So it's not here and I know that I did mark that location as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you're talking about another location now. I'm asking you to focus on this map in the area of Alipasino Polje, where you lived. You did not mark any military target in Alipasino Polje during your Galic evidence; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, now when I mentioned Alipasino Polje, I wonder if you heard me, I said that Trg Medjunarodnog Prijateljstva Square up to PTT Engineering is -- it's all Alipasino Polje, and up to the land survey institute, all of that is Alipasino Polje, and the section that we are talking about. So from Ante Babica, if you can see that street, and then to the left, Alipasino Polje --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all the way to the land survey institute, all of that is Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me get an answer to my question and then I'll ask you to mark if we need to. Yes or no, did you mark any military target on the compound of Alipasino Polje in your Galic testimony? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did mark it, at least three or four targets were in Alipasino Polje from where they fired at us. So they had to be marked, but I can't see it on this map here now. It's not recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that you recall marking military targets in Alipasino Polje during your Galic testimony, but those markings are not on this map that's now before us?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as -- I can't see the markings, but I know that there were locations from which they fired at us and that constituted potential military targets. And a little while ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in this trial we talked about the mortar nest, 120-millimetres, here next to the Prvi Maj School.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, my question is purely limited to whether or not you marked these locations you're talking about during your Galic testimony. Did you or did you not mark these locations in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I should have done it, that I must have done it. Why it's not on this map, I don't know, but I cannot remember with 100 per cent certainty to be completely frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 30685. That's Galic Exhibit 1D1814.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30685 receives number P6531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention to paragraph 22 of your statement. You say: "I was not aware of the Ilidza Brigade deploying mortars on the grounds of the theological college from September 1992 to August 1994. I would have known had they been there." My question is: Are you certain about the fact that there were no mortars on the grounds of the theological faculty?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there were no mortars in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your evidence in your statement is not in the school. I think we all have figured out at this stage that it's not possible to fire a mortar with -- inside a building. Your evidence was: "... deploying mortars on the grounds of the theological college ..." Are you quite certain that there were no mortars deployed on the grounds of the theological college or theological faculty?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it that I didn't see them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said: "I would have known had they been there ..." What did you mean by that statement: "I would have known had they been there"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, number one, had I not seen them. Had I seen them, I would have known of their existence there. Quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just be clear. That's not what the language says. The language doesn't say: If I haven't seen them, I'm not aware of them. Of course if you do not see something you cannot -- it suggests that if they would have been there even though you personally may not have seen them, that you would have known it by other means if they would have been there. That's what the language suggests. Is that a proper understanding of this part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think -- I'm saying I really did not see them and I cannot say that I saw them if I did not see them. That is, I mean, I think that the most correct answer would be that I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you said more than that. You said: "I would have known had they been there." If you don't see something from your position, you may consider it extremely likely that you would have been informed about it even if you have not seen it with your own eyes. That's what the text suggests. Is that also your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I mean, it could be interpreted that way and it could be expected, the way you put it just now. But because of many circumstances, many developments in the zone all the time, the zone of a brigade that had these 36 offensives coming from the enemy, believe me, it's hundreds of incidents per day, people being killed, wounded, all sorts of things were happening, I mean all sorts of things. Even if I were a computer, I wouldn't be able to know all of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not just talking about events. We are talking about mortars being positioned at the grounds of the theological faculty. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please see P6509. It's a panoramic photo taken from the faculty of theology.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the first question I'll ask you, Mr. Mijatovic, is a previous Defence witness has given evidence --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just a second, please. I'm not Mijanovic. I am Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misspoke, but yes, I know that you are Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or it was the interpreter, the interpreter that made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Possibly. We're all speaking very quickly but we all realise that you are Mr. Mijatovic. A previous witness has given evidence that this photo is a view from the theological faculty. Can I ask you to look at it and tell me whether you agree.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the witness also gave evidence that sometime -- I'm sorry, that the location marked as M1, that paved area adjacent to the building, indicates where four to five mortars were placed up until approximately the end of 1992. Do you accept that this contradicts your evidence that there were no mortars at this location?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right now we'll be going back to my statement here. In 1992, I mean, I said that from June, July, and August -- in fact, I spent three months in hospital. Then I was in this rear unit, and then after that I was assistant commander for morale and information and religious affairs, where it is very realistic to expect that I did not know and that I could not have known of all of these things. I mean, all these others who were saying this, they probably have arguments for that. Obviously for 1992, I could not have known about that. It doesn't make it any more difficult or any less difficult, but objectively that's what I said and that's what I stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The witness then provided evidence that M2 on the screen in front of you indicates the meadow or the green meadow behind the theological faculty, and that's where the mortars were moved at the end of 1992. Do you accept that this evidence contradicts your evidence that there were no mortars on the grounds of the theological college or faculty?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the area of the faculty of theology, now what is that? The zone is 5 metres, 10 metres from the faculty of theology. One could conclude, as far as I could see, that it could be M2. That could be 100 metres away from the faculty of theology and then there are other buildings there in between. I mean -- so what you're asking is very relative about the area of the faculty of theology. After all, this witness - if it's a valid witness -- I mean, I cannot say, not that I don't know. I cannot confirm or deny things that that person said. It wouldn't be right. It wouldn't be proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, hold on --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you about what I know. What I know, that's what I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've just said that "I don't know," but yet in your statement which is now in evidence as D468 you said: "I would have known had they been there ..." That statement is no longer true, is it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the contrary, it is true and how. All the time. I mean, we can just play with words here, but I am saying -- and all of it boils down to it being correct that I did not know. Practically I had no way of knowing because I was not in that area during that period -- or rather, I was there very little. You know where the command is, it's not even close to Nedzarici or the faculty of theology, and that's where I spent time roughly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have -- if I now properly understand your testimony, I would have expected in your statement: For the latter part of 1992, I would not even have known if they were there because I wasn't around and I was -- you were, I think, hospitalised or -- that that would come closer to what you are telling us now than what we read in your statement. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, it's the same. I still stand by each and every word I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not agree with me. Then I have one other question. You disputed or at least you raised a question about what the grounds of the theological faculty would be. If you would look at that photograph which is still in front of you and look at the position of M2, would you know whether there ever had been any mortars there in the -- after 1992? So position M2. If you know, tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most correct answer is: I'm not sure. It's been a long time, all of this has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't -- you can't tell us with an adequate level of certainty. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I wanted to switch to a different topic. I want to draw your attention to paragraph 29 of your statement in this case where you address an incident referred to as G13. It involves a modified air bomb that landed on Safeta Hadzica Street. Do you remember the incident that I'm referring to? Please, a simple yes or no will do.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do I understand your evidence correctly that this air bomb was launched in response to what you referred to as "an all-out Muslim offensive"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never stated that that air bomb was launched in response to a Muslim offensive, no. I don't even know who it was that launched that air bomb. I know from the media, from television, Muslim television at the time, we found out that this bomb fell. It's not that we -- I mean, I just said that the time coincided with this all-out Muslim offensive. I never could have stated that that bomb was a response to that. From the media --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I remember that very well, Muslim media, Muslim television, that's where I found out about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please have D468 up on the screen and can we please go to paragraph 29, which I believe is the second-to-last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can now see your statement, paragraph 29 of your statement in both languages. Let me ask you this. Paragraph 29 you say: "It was explained to me that on 26 May 1995 an incident occurred in Safeta Hadzica Street and that according to the findings of Muslim police the trajectory of the projectile was west/south-west ..." My question is: Who was it that explained to you that information?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that over here it could be heard from the previous trials, that's the only way I could have received this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that no one --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what I said -- sorry, sorry. What I said that I heard during the war from the media, or rather, Muslim TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could have -- please have 65 ter 30684 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is your statement which was admitted in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could go to paragraph 26, which should be the third from the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will read it to you while it's being brought up on our screens. So your Karadzic statement about the same event says: "It was explained to me on the 26th of June, 1995, an incident occurred in Safeta Hadzica Street and that according to the findings of the Muslim police the trajectory of the projectile was west/south-west ..." You were incorrect about the date in the Karadzic case, were you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that precisely here we see the exact date, the 26th of June. It started, this strong Muslim offensive, on the 16th of June. It went on almost for months. So on the 16th of June, one of the strongest Muslim offensives was launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you were reading from the Karadzic statement which is on our screen now, because then the quote is not exact. Could you please re-read page 75, line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll just read the quote again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see that there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "It was explained to me that on 26 June 1995 an incident occurred in Safeta Hadzica Street and that according to the findings of the Muslim police the trajectory of the projectile was west/south-west ..." In the Mladic statement you said that it was explained to you that the incident in Safeta Hadzica Street occurred on the 26th of May. In the Karadzic case you said it was explained to you that that incident occurred on the 26th of June. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously the only mistake here is a typo, a typo. The months are different, that's all. Because the fiercest offensive, the most massive one, the strongest one in the war started on the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that this offensive started on the 16th of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's go back to your Mladic statement, D468, again to paragraph 29, and there you say: "I would like to point out that on 26 May 1995 a fierce Muslim offensive was underway against all lines of the SRK, mostly against the Ilidza Brigade ..." Do you remember putting that in your statement for this case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, Mr. Prosecutor, things were confused when typing up the month. That is so clear. It's just a typo, to be precise, a typographical error. June is the correct month. I repeat that the strongest offensive launched against Serb Sarajevo, especially Serb Ilidza, it started on the 16th of June, and there's no dilemma in my mind. I remember that and everybody remembers that, so it's just a typo. The month was called May instead of June. The year is the same and everything else is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, you signed this statement on the 10th of May, just a matter of weeks ago. Did you review this statement prior to signing it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I reviewed it but you know that mistakes may happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you first wait to hear what the question by Mr. Groome is. He started asking whether you had reviewed. I think you have answered that. Mr. Groome, and then you were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were you when you reviewed your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That first statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- the 10th of May, when you signed your statement, where were you when you signed your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 10th of May, 2014?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, this year. I was together with the gentleman from the team, but not these two here, their colleague in Pale. That's where I signed that statement. Their colleague came to Pale and -- I mean, it was with him, yes. But also, again there was quite a bit of a rush. There were several witnesses, if I can put it that way, so no wonder that the months were interchanged here, May, June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So is it your evidence that you did not have adequate time to review your statement before you signed it on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, relatively enough time, but obviously this mistake slipped in. Whatever I were to say, there is a mistake, but there is no dilemma at any moment that this strongest initiative -- offensive started on the 16th of June. And so what is correct is what is stated in Mr. Karadzic's statement. Although let us be clear, in May there were attacks as well and all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. You said there were several witnesses at the time. Were you the first one who were invited to sign or were you the last one or how many witnesses were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, actually, I was alone, in fact, when I gave this statement and when I signed it, but then others were waiting, for instance, for their turn, but I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many witnesses were there waiting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been two at least, as far as I can remember, at least two. And I was the third one, if I'm not mistaken, on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time did you take to carefully read the details of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, methodologically a page is read three to five minutes. That is proven by science. Now, there can be an entire text and then a person would have to do this a lot more seriously, say, you would need 10 or 15 minutes for a page. And then if you were to analyse every full stop and comma, then perhaps it would be even longer. So it's hard for me to say how much time I needed for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I asked you how much time there was given or you took, not on what it would have required, but how much time did you take or were you given to re-read this statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Mr. President, just to read it without a thorough analysis and comparison, obviously I can do it very fast. But if I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you what you could have done. I'm simply asking you: How much time did you take? Did you take two minutes? Ten minutes? An hour? How much time did you take to review it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly to do it thoroughly I'd need half an hour at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now for the third time have to establish that you are not answering my question. I understand this as unwillingness to tell me how much time you had. Or did you just sign it even without having read it or just going through the pages? What was it? How much time was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I do apologise. That's not the interpretation that I received. The interpretation I received was how much time I would need otherwise to read this. I said half an hour, so that's what I was told, right? I mean, that's what the interpretation was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, you're blaming our interpreters to, most likely, have misinterpreted three times, because I asked you the same question three times, and if they misinterpreted it, especially if they misinterpreted it for three times, then of course that would be something to seriously consider. We may check that. Was it translated, my question to you, three times how much time you would have needed? Or was it translated to you that I asked you three times now how much time you have taken to read it, how much time you took? And I want an answer to that last question. And whatever it was, one minute, three hours, the only thing I want that information to hear --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the most correct question. I do apologise. I apologise to the workers who are working here. Maybe I misunderstood. I'm not narrow-minded. Say between half an hour and an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You took between half an hour and an hour to review before you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't look at the watch, but according to my recollection it might have been that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it according to your recollection or might it have been? Was it between half an hour and an hour or could it have been shorter or even longer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's this. Again, it's guess-work on my part because I didn't look at the watch, so all of it is, I mean, hypothetical thinking in terms of how long it lasted because I didn't look at the watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, so I've read you the same sentence in your Karadzic testimony and your Mladic testimony. In the Karadzic testimony you said the event that you were giving information on occurred on the 26th of June. In your Mladic statement you say that that event occurred on the 26th of May. Which is the correct date? Which incident are you -- which -- what's the date of the incident you're providing evidence about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly what the date is because that was -- well, that was 1995 so that was 19 years ago. Is that right? I just know, as far as I can remember and that's why I explained this, that it could have been the 26th of May, this is the time of the strong enemy offensive. And this date here in President Karadzic's case was communicated to me then. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- the problem I have is that the date keeps changing. Now you say: "... the 26th of May, this is the time of the strong enemy offensive." Didn't you minutes ago, sitting in this courtroom, tell us that that strong offensive started on the 16th of June?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that, no denying that, it started on the 16th of June, the offensive, and it went on for a month. I'm sorry, I didn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about an event that's referred to as G10 in both your Mladic and Karadzic statements. I draw you to paragraph 28 of your Mladic statement. You -- the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe we could call that up for the witness, that's D468, paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last sentence of this paragraph reads: "I do not know any other details about the incident." And I'll wait until you can see that and ask you to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it and it is clear that it was explained to me back then in the courtroom about the incident, as was the case with the previous incident on the 13th. Either the Prosecution or Defence explained to me what we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have anything on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nor do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps only the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now we see it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So at the end, the last sentence you say: "I do not know any other details about the incident." Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as I understand this relatively brief paragraph, you provide four facts: One, an incident allegedly occurred in Hrasnica in April 1995; two, the command of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army was located in the centre of Hrasnica; three, according to your intelligence sources, there was a 120-millimetre mortar located at the place of impact; and four, the mortar was under the command of Fikret Pljevljak. Do you agree that that is all of the information that you provide in this relatively short paragraph? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not all of the information --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I remember mentioning something else and I'm surprised not to see it here, although I know that Mr. Ivetic must have forwarded it to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the sentence that says: "I do not know any other details about the incident." As of the 10th -- that you signed on the 10th of May, as of today that statement is no longer correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ivetic forwarded you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the information stating that in Hrasnica in addition to the machine-gun nest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I intervene. Whatever Mr. Ivetic may have sent to us, yes or no, is not part of the question. On the 10th of May you signed a statement in which, apart from the four facts mentioned, you explicitly state: "I do not know any other details about the incident." Which means that on the 10th of May you clearly said: I have no further knowledge. And Mr. Groome was focusing on that statement given on the 10th of May and he would like to know - Mr. Groome, if I understood you well - that at that point in time you had no knowledge whether that's true, 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would not be correct at that moment. There was other information, though, in circulation and you cannot recall everything off-the-cuff at any given moment. Anyone is able to recollect additional things. That's what I'm trying to say, that there were around 80 heavy pieces there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no -- I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I said so in Karadzic. I don't know why it's not here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to say what you knew more about it. So you stated something at that point in time, not saying: I am unaware whether or other details do not come to my mind. You said: I do not know any other details about the incident. And you tell us now that that's not -- may have been true at the time, but certainly you remembered details since then. Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So on the 21st of May, 11 days later, we receive a seven-page document, nearly as long as the statement, which purports to be additional information that you provided on three days, the 16th, the 18th, and the 21st of May. Now, I want to read you a section of that document, bearing in mind your statement: "I do not know any other details" apart from what is in your statement and your evidence that there was a 120-millimetre mortar in Hrasnica. The information provided on the 21st of May has additional information for paragraph 28 and states: [As read] "The witness would add that Hrasnica had numerous military targets, including three tanks, five transporters, one multi-rocket-launcher, two 105-millimetre howitzers, four 76-millimetre guns, dozens of 82-millimetre mortars, dozens of 60-millimetre mortars, and dozens of 120-millimetre mortars." Do you accept that in the 11 days between you signed the statement and we received this note of additional information, that is a -- very significant additional information has been provided regarding the amount of weapons in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you signed your Mladic statement on the 10th of May. It was the product of five days of interviews in addition to however many times you were interviewed by the Karadzic Defence. Do you accept that all you talk about in those statements is the 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not only about that. As we are discussing this, in the process of providing answers, things are coming back. During the last Muslim offensive, it was shown on their TV that they had a 24-barrel multiple rocket-launcher just above Hrasnica where they opened fire from -- upon us during the last offensive. And I wasn't able to recall that before now. And their TV broadcast it, confirming it. Hence, you shouldn't be surprised when someone recollects something which had been suppressed for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, may I ask you how many days have you been interviewed in April, July, October, and December of last year, on the basis of which this statement was compiled which you signed on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three days for sure, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the time-frame from April to December 2013, as it is written in your statement. And you say in this long time-period, all the details you have provided now didn't come up to your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that it didn't come up to my mind, but, for example, there was something more important at that particular point in time and unless you write it down, just like everyone else, it's difficult. We remember as much as we suppress, otherwise the brain would implod e from all the information we have received during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not interested in any explanation how a brain and a memory works. If you just would have not mentioned these details, that would be one story, but you explicitly said: "I do not know any other details about the incident." "I do not know any other details." After months of interview on many days, and now all of a sudden it comes to your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is what the point of a particular question is. If someone is asking me about a particular alleged incident - and I believe I describe it as such - then it is only normal that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stop you again because you are not answering my question. How does it come about or did it come about that this sentence is included: "I do not know any other details." And now you provide us all of a sudden with many other details, very precise details. Why did you say: "I do not know any other details"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I stand by it. I do not have specific information regarding that incident. All the rest is secondary, things that occurred in our theatre of war, and I wanted to say to the Chamber and the Prosecutor is that I wanted to paint an image of the size of forces we were in conflict with and what things were happening, what kind of assets and weapons were used against us at Ilidza alone, and the importance of this particular incident is up to the Chamber to decide. However, it is up to me to say that they indeed had all the assets at their disposal that I am talking about now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now you say: All the rest is secondary. Is it hearsay? Did anybody provide you with this information during your interview or what has happened that you are now able to give all the details in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, direct knowledge or hearsay. Direct knowledge means that I would have to go to the enemy side to see each of the assets or take photographs of them in order to have direct knowledge. To my mind, all of the information we had concerning different sources, like our observers or captured enemy soldiers, et cetera, all that all suddenly becomes hearsay as if unreliable or incorrect. I can't have first-hand knowledge unless I go to the enemy side. I think it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be asked to move away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, whatever I tried to compare after the war with my original knowledge actually tallied and that information came from enemy sources --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. I have heard enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this proofing note, 65 ter 30696.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30696 -- I apologise, is it 96 or 86? 96, receives number P6532, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I would have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That concludes my examination of the witness. I don't want the Chamber to have a false impression of what's just happened, and I bring to the Chamber's attention that the witness does, in at least his Galic testimony that I can recall, mention some other assets in Hrasnica, certainly nothing on the order of what we see in P6532, but if it assists the Chamber in the Prosecution pulling together those different excerpts so the Chamber can compare, we'd be more than happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would have a few questions, very few questions. Perhaps it's better that I put them now so that you have a better opportunity to prepare during the break for any further questions. Witness, Hrasnica, when you are referring to Hrasnica and when you say that there was a command centre in -- command of the BH Army was in the centre of Hrasnica, Hrasnica, you're referring to a village; is that correctly understood? Not. What does it then mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was interpreted to me that that is where the command of the ABiH was. The command of the 104th Brigade of the so-called ABiH was there, so there's a difference between a brigade and the army, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just read from your statement: "As far as I know, the command of the BH Army was in the centre of Hrasnica ..." That's what your statement says in English, but apart from that, that was not the focus of my question. Hrasnica is a village; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a rather large settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A settlement of 500 metres long? A thousand metres long? Could you give us -- from maps I've seen until now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can approximate. I think the settlement had over 10.000 inhabitants and it is at least 3 kilometres in length by some 2 kilometres in width. It even had a second division soccer team, which is a sign of its size. It is a large settlement, not a village. Perhaps a town would be a better way to describe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- 2 kilometres in width, you said, 3 kilometres in length, do you mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean the built-up area, so the populated where we find houses? Or do you -- are you talking about the area including fields surrounding this settlement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I refer to, I think it is the built-up area, the urban area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the parties are invited to carefully look at their maps where the built-up area seems to be considerably smaller than what I at least have seen until now. Now, when you describe, apart from the 120-millimetre mortar nest near to the point of impact and if you would describe all the rest of the armament that you said was in Hrasnica, was that all in the settlement itself where these howitzers -- or were they in the wider area of Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some in the settlement itself and around it. As for APCs or tanks, you know they can move from one place to the next. It is difficult for me to limit each of those to a single location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The fixed ones, where were they? Could you, in line with the list you gave, tell us exactly, for example, the mortars where -- the dozens of mortars, where were they? Could you tell us where they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right at this moment, let me try to recall it all, although it would take time. I have managed to remember many things, though. I know they were in the outskirts of Hrasnica. I know that, for example, their multiple rocket-launcher was in the outskirts of the settlement itself. I discovered it and I asked that it be engaged. For the most part, they were in the outskirts, but the nests moved places. It is only logical. If they were observed by our observers, they become a target and then they move. Any assets that could be moved were never left in a single place for the entire war. It is simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I'm just focusing on the day of at least the time-frame of this incident. Could you tell us the dozens of mortars of the various calibres, could you give us six, seven, eight positions where they were to be found? Yes, in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In April, for the most part -- well, it's difficult for me to recall right now. I would like to be fair and correct. I can't say exactly. In principle, they moved inside that area. As for any specific locations, I can't, not after this much time, it would be unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All those dozens and dozens of mortars were moving around all the time? If you have them by the tens in the various calibres, they would nevertheless change position again and again? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't understand me well. It doesn't only concern mortars. If you followed, I said that it also had to do with tanks, APCs, guns, multiple rocket-launchers, howitzers, and mortars. They would stay in a place for a period and then, for safety reasons, they moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I asked you about the mortars. My previous question was: Could you tell us the dozens of mortars of the various calibres, could you give us six, seven, eight positions where they were to be found in April 1995? And if you then answer dealing with other armaments, then of course I do not think that I got an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try to deal with the mortars only. I know that in the firewood warehouse they had a nest for a 120-millimetre asset. I think it was at the beginning of the conflict and we were shelled frequently from there. I also know that they had it at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I'm trying, I'm trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You're not trying at all because I'm asking you about April 1995 and you're telling me about the beginning of the conflict. So I'm not saying that you're not trying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the beginning of 1995. I meant the beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the beginning of the conflict, but we may verify that as well, whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it's a mistake. I thought the beginning of -- because it's in April, it's sort of characteristic of 1995. That's what I mean. They were in the firewood warehouse. They were near the road up to Igman, on the right-hand side, so that's two. There was a mortar near the place of the incident, so that's three. So I can recall these three places right here and now, and that's all I can be precise and confident of. There were some further up close to their point at Igman. There was also a 120-millimetre mortar nest there and that was also in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break. We have only very short to go after the break and, Mr. Ivetic, I can imagine that it would not be sufficient time for you for a further examination. But we take the break. We would like to see you back at five minutes past 2.00 and we will then, to start with, have ten minutes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. There's no need to seek eye contact with anyone else in this -- no, Mr. Mladic is supposed not to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can you give us an impression on how much time you would approximately need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm close to 15 minutes. I'm going to try and see if I can squeeze it into the ten minutes that we have so we can dispense with the witness coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then of course the question remains how much time Mr. Groome then would still need but okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now further examine you, Mr. Mijatovic. Try to focus on his questions and answer them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day again, sir. I would like to return to Hrasnica and the situation on the ground in 1995 in Ilidza. How often did Ilidza receive incoming fire from the ABiH forces located in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often. They used powerful assets. I think I said on Friday that my brigade alone had sustained 460 people killed, several hundred wounded, and in addition to the Ilidza Brigade, there were other units in Ilidza which also sustained many losses. I think we had the highest number of killed personnel in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think in the entire Yugoslav theatre of war, the Ilidza part was affected the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the incoming fire that was coming in from Hrasnica, would that level of fire change during the time-period of cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be fair, in terms of intensity during cease-fires, it did change but it doesn't mean it stopped all together. Never did the enemy side honour any cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What kind of ordnance specifically was used by the ABiH in Hrasnica against Ilidza during 1995 that you recall?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be specific, in 1995 they opened fire from all available assets, starting with cannons of different calibres, howitzers, mortars, multiple rocket-launchers. There was an example when nine people were killed nearby the municipal building and over 20 were wounded. They were all wounded by a multiple rocket-launcher. They had 120-millimetre, 82-millimetre mortars, 60-millimetre mortars, howitzers, 105, 125-millimetre. They also used the Sultan, as they called it, it is 155-millimetre asset. And they also had infantry weapons of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you, sir, you have now identified an incident where nine people were killed nearby the municipal building and over 20 were wounded. Was that the only such instance of targeting from Hrasnica upon Ilidza which resulted in civilian casualties or were there other such incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just wondering how this arises from cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it arises from the questioning of the number of assets that are in Hrasnica and establishing the reliability of the witness's testimony as to the list of additional assets that he has identified in proofing and in his direct examination on Friday, which was challenged by the Prosecution in cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just say something, you're talking about civilians. The answer said "nine people." It didn't say "civilians." You are now introducing the concept of civilians, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment. Let me just scroll up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at page 95, line 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. It should be "persons" not "civilians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. Your time is relatively limited. I leave it a bit to you. It requires a bit of inventivity to link it to the cross-examination, but I'm not going to stop you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's move on for the moment. You were asked during cross-examination about the approximately 200 soldiers arrested for disciplinary matters. What knowledge did you have of General Mladic and the Main Staff and their position as to discipline of soldiers among the lower commands?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander General Mladic insisted on discipline all the time and on sticking to the Geneva Conventions, implementing the customs of war, he requested that whoever violated discipline be prosecuted, that civilian facilities and religious facilities in the city not be targeted, that civilians not be targeted. And I'm proud of having such a commander and such other commanders in the corps, who in addition to defending their own people also took care about the other ethnic group and in particular the civilians from this other ethnic group, even though they were our enemies. And when I said that I am proud, I remain proud that from Ilidza --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Mr. Ivetic, you are invited to, if the witness comes to general sweeping statements which have got nothing to do with the knowledge of facts personally observed by him, that you would perhaps interrupt him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, today at temporary transcript page 20, when talking about aerial bombs, you said: "All weapons imply certain deviations if that is what you had in mind." I would like to have you explain what type of weapons you are referring to when you say "all weapons."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind all weapons when I said this because there is no weapon for which anyone could guarantee. Even those who take part in sports competitions do not always get the best marks. That's what I had in mind. So there is no tool that you can guarantee would have not a single percentage of deviation and that deviation is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'll not deduct it from your time. The issue raised by the Prosecution, apparently now again by Mr. Ivetic, is whether these aerial bombs are any less precise than what is the normal range of imprecision, of which we know a lot about mortars and et cetera, whether they are similarly inaccurate in -- when fired or whether there's any difference. That is the -- apparently the issue. Could you tell us whether you have any knowledge about any difference between precision, aerial bombs compared with other weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is some difference. To be fair, there is some difference between aerial bombs, even though that's conventional weapon like other conventional weapons, but there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is the difference? Are they more or are they less precise than, well, let's say, mortars or cannons or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, once again, to be fair, they're less precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The rocket engines attached to the modified aerial bombs by the VRS, do you know if they were tested before being so attached and used?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecution asked you about the amount of explosives in those aerial bombs that were used. Do you have any knowledge to be able to compare the amount of explosives in those bombs with the amount of explosives in bombs dropped by NATO aircraft or by Tomahawks on the territory of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MIJATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the bombs that NATO dropped on the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska were incomparably heavier, 10 to 20 times heavier than the bombs which the Serbs used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I complete my redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you one additional question. Could you give us -- the bombs NATO dropped, what type of bombs were they? We have not heard much about that, that's the reason, since you appear to have knowledge about -- what type, what ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were mostly bombs enriched with depleted uranium. You know what sorts of consequences uranium had on the Serbian population in and around Sarajevo. That's the most horrible form of bombing that we could have experienced because to this day people are dying as a consequence of these bombs containing depleted uranium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but could you say it was this or that type of bomb or the bombs fired by NATO dropped on the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had an occasion to see the bombs or one that was dug out from 12 metres below a house owned by my relatives. It was taken out and fortunately it never exploded. So the rapid intervention unit had to dig. It was 12 metres deep in the ground and it was a huge bomb, much bigger than the ones that we had and that had 250 kilos. I know that Tomahawks were used, I know that likewise very destructive 30- and 40-millimetre shells were used. I had a chance to see them because they hit our positions above Blazuj, above the transformer station that was mentioned. It's a part of Igman which is called Golo Brdo and that was precisely where they would pass 20 metres below us and go on to the other side. And not knowing that they contained uranium, I held some of them in my hands. How that would be reflected in my health, we shall see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
